description: We’re Bay of Orbits, a team from Dhaka, Bangladesh, made up of students passionate about technology, science, space, and building things together. Our team has skills in full-stack development, programming, Python, research, data, graphics, and video editing. We’re interested in using NASA data and technology to solve real-world problems, especially in agriculture and environmental sustainability.
summary:
AgriOrbit is a bilingual (English and Bangla) web app that helps farmers and agriculture extension officers in Bangladesh plan a full-year, three-season crop rotation for a climate that has already changed.

NASA data shows how far the seasons have shifted. In Rangpur, the pre-monsoon season now gets 42% of the year's rain, up from 34% in 2001–2010, and winters are 0.5°C warmer. Many farmers still plant by the old calendar.

AgriOrbit combines NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP, MODIS, NASADEM and GRACE-FO data with BARI and BRRI crop guidance and the farmer's own priority: saving water, soil health, lower cost or lower risk. It compares the farmer's current rotation with better options, scores 37 crops across all 64 districts, and explains every score with a rule the user can read. An interactive map shows rainfall, erosion-prone land and long-term water storage for each district.

This matters because a wrong crop choice can cost a farming family a whole season. AgriOrbit turns free NASA observations into clear, explained options, and the farmer and the local agriculture officer make the final decision.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS
AgriOrbit is a bilingual (English and Bangla) web app that helps farmers and agriculture extension officers in Bangladesh plan a full-year, three-season crop rotation (Rabi, Kharif-1 and Kharif-2) for a changing climate.

  1. NASA observes. For all 64 districts we use NASA POWER (daily weather, crop water need with the Hargreaves ET₀ method, and climate history since 2001), GPM IMERG V07 (satellite rainfall), SMAP (soil moisture), MODIS (vegetation), NASADEM (elevation and slope) and GRACE/GRACE-FO JPL mascons (long-term total water storage). Open-Meteo covers the 2–3 days before NASA data arrives. Every value on screen shows its source and whether it is live, cached or a snapshot.
  2. Explainable SI scores the options. A transparent rule-based engine scores 37 crops using BARI and BRRI guidance (duration, water need, optimal temperature, key risks), current NASA conditions, and the farmer's priority: save water, soil health, lower cost or lower risk. The "Explain why" view shows each rule, for example "30-day rain < 50 mm and soil moisture < 0.15 → high-water crops −15".
  3. A whole-year rotation. AgriOrbit compares the farmer's current rotation with better options. Rotation rules avoid repeating a plant family, which breaks pest and disease cycles, and add a nitrogen-fixing legume such as lentil or mungbean when the soil needs it. A What-If simulator shows how scores change under different conditions.
  4. An interactive map shows GPM rainfall, where GPM and NASA POWER disagree, erosion-prone land (share steeper than 5°), elevation, GRACE water-storage trends with a time slider, and soil moisture. Hotspot outlines follow written rules shown on the map.
  5. The farmer decides. AgriOrbit gives options and reasons, not orders, and every advisory asks the user to confirm with their local Sub-Assistant Agriculture Officer.

BENEFITS

  • Shows farmers, in their own language, how their district's seasons have already shifted. In Rangpur, the pre-monsoon season now gets 42% of the year's rain instead of 34%, and winters are 0.5°C warmer than in 2001–2010.
  • Suggests rotations that save irrigation water, restore soil nitrogen and lower risk, compared with repeating water-hungry crops.
  • Every score can be checked, so farmers and officers can trust it or disagree with it.
  • Free and web-based, built on open NASA data.

INTENDED IMPACT
Bangladesh's planting calendars were written for an older climate. A wrong crop choice can cost a farming family a whole season. AgriOrbit aims to give farmers and extension officers a simple, honest tool for planning around the climate that exists now, and to help reduce groundwater pumping in dry regions by pointing to lower-water options.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

  • Front end: React web app with a Leaflet interactive map, hosted on Vercel, in English and Bangla.
  • Data pipeline: Python (requests, NumPy, xarray, netCDF4) and NASA AppEEARS, GES DISC and PO.DAAC through Earthdata Login, updated automatically by GitHub Actions.
  • Data: NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP, MODIS, NASADEM, GRACE/GRACE-FO, Open-Meteo, UN OCHA district boundaries, BARI and BRRI crop guidance.
  • AI-assisted coding and writing tools, with all code and data reviewed by the team. No AI-generated data is used.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

  • It plans a full year of three seasons instead of recommending a single crop.
  • It uses explainable SI: rules anyone can read instead of a black-box model.
  • It shows disagreement between datasets instead of hiding it. During Cyclone Arnab's remnant rain in late October 2026, GPM recorded far more rain over Rangpur than NASA POWER did, and the map shows both.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

  • Scale honesty: GRACE's native resolution is about 3°, so Bangladesh falls into only 5 independent mascons. We show those regions rather than pretending to have 64 district values.
  • Data limits: NASA POWER rainfall has processing breaks, so Field Shift compares when rain falls rather than total amounts. We found that district headquarter points fall on urban pixels, so the crop-greenness layer is held back until it uses cropland pixels.
  • Local fit: Bangladesh rarely sees frost, so we track cold injury below 10°C, which harms Boro seedlings and potato.
  • Farmer needs: Bangla language, simple screens, and the farmer's own priorities.
  • Responsibility: missing data is shown as missing, never estimated, and the tool does not replace local agricultural experts.

NEXT STEPS
Cropland-masked NDVI time series to detect bare-field periods, soil data (ISRO SoilGrids), ECOSTRESS heat stress, a Methods page, SMS alerts for farmers without smartphones, and pilot testing with agriculture officers.
